items.title: Did Ukraine Use A Mothership To Launch Its Sea Drone Attack On Russian Ships in Benghazi?
items.summary:
The uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that attacked a Russian Navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday were launched from a mothership at sea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) claimed on Monday . The SBU’s comments appear to be the first official confirmation that Ukraine has ever used a vessel to deliver USVs for an attack. Still, its statement doesn’t prove a mothership was actually used, as there is good reason for misdirecting with such a claim, but it certainly seems more probable than not.

The SBU account also conflicts with statements made on Sunday about the origin of the attacks. Libyan officials claimed that the strikes were launched from a base in their country , while there were also claims , later denied, that the USVs sailed from Albania. For years, we have raised the possibility that Ukraine was using motherships to launch USVs, especially in the Black Sea. In the case of the Benghazi attacks, we directly mentioned that the strikes could have originated from a ship as opposed to the shore.

The Russian corvette Merkury seen rolled over on its side at a port in Benghazi, Libya, in a satellite image collected by Vantor on Monday. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) 

New Details On The Benghazi Sea Drone Attacks 

As we reported yesterday , the Project 20380 Steregushchiy class corvette Merkury sank after being struck by USVs while moored at a dock in the port of Benghazi. A cargo ship was also struck by USVs while in the waters outside of Benghazi.

The SBU provided new details on Monday about these attacks.

items.t: Did Ukraine Use A Mothership To Launch Its Sea Drone Attack On Russian Ships in Benghazi?

items.title: New Mexico faces federal lawsuit after rejecting military spouse’s law license
items.summary:
New Mexico must face a federal lawsuit over its rejection of a military spouse’s law license application, a decision the Justice Department called an “important victory for military families.” 

Judge Kea Riggs of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico on Thursday denied motions filed by the New Mexico Supreme Court and the New Mexico Board of Bar Examiners to dismiss a case involving the professional license portability provisions in the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, or SCRA. 

The Justice Department filed the suit in June after the New Mexico Board of Bar Examiners ruled against admitting Liam Lees, a military spouse who sought to practice law in New Mexico when his wife was transferred to Holloman Air Force Base in Alamogordo. 

Lees studied law in the United Kingdom and received a master of laws degree from William and Mary Law School in Virginia in 2024. The New Mexico bar argued, however, that Lees was ineligible to practice in the state because he did not meet its rules, which require bar applicants to have earned a Juris Doctor or Bachelor of Laws and Letters degree.  

Lees, who is licensed to practice in Texas, Washington and Maryland, sought a waiver to the requirement but was denied. During his application proceedings, he also argued that he qualified for the bar under the SCRA’s license portability provisions. 

The Justice Department took the case on June 11, the first-ever lawsuit to enforce the SCRA’s professional license portability provisions, according to the department. 

“Military families should be able to make New Mexico their home…
items.t: New Mexico faces federal lawsuit after rejecting military spouse’s law license

items.title: USS Theodore Roosevelt replaces USS George Washington in the Middle East
items.summary:
The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is officially operating in the Middle East “to support maritime security and stability,” according to the U.S. Navy.

The ship’s arrival comes amid the ongoing war with Iran, which later this week will enter its ninth month. The U.S. imposed new Iran-related financial sanctions Monday, while Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it would use all of its tools to confront the U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Roosevelt left its homeport in San Diego, California, on Sept. 27. Navy officials told family members of loved ones aboard that ship to expect at least a seven-month-long deployment.

The carrier replaced the USS George Washington following its three-month stint in the area. 

The Washington arrived in the Middle East on Aug. 19 to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln after a historic 10-month deployment that saw the crew go 286 days without a port call.

The Washington, which deployed from its Yokosuka, Japan, base in May, left the Middle East and is currently operating in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of operations, a Navy release confirmed. The carrier’s stay in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility was significantly shorter than the Lincoln’s, which operated in the area for approximately seven months.

Other carriers’ deployment cycles in the Middle East have varied, including the future timeframe for carriers recently deployed to the area.

The aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford was sent to the Middle East in February and left in April, a relatively brief stop. But the Ford, which deployed for nearly…
items.t: USS Theodore Roosevelt replaces USS George Washington in the Middle East

items.title: Trump reluctantly orders Army to pause detonation of unstable ammunition
items.summary:
President Donald Trump on Monday said he is putting a pause on the U.S. Army’s controversial plan to detonate unstable ammunition stores in Iowa following an onslaught of criticism from local communities and lawmakers concerned about the long-term effects of the operation. 

Trump said he wanted to move forward with the controlled blasts, which had already been delayed multiple times, but he was putting the decision in the hands of the courts. The Army won’t move forward with the detonation without agreement from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit and Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand, Trump said.

If the ammunition becomes unstable enough to detonate on its own during the pause, Trump said he “would be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction.”

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump announced on social media.

Trump blamed former President Barack Obama’s administration for improper storage of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Military Times has not been able to verify this claim. 

The Army announced last week that it needed to destroy more than 9,000 pounds of degraded lead azide, a highly sensitive chemical compound used in military blasting caps and detonators. According to the Army, the increasingly cold winter weather makes…
items.t: Trump reluctantly orders Army to pause detonation of unstable ammunition

items.title: Under Hegseth, the OSS rides again — kind of
items.summary:
The Office of Strategic Services rides again — at least in name.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth resurrected the OSS, the intelligence and commando wing of the U.S. military that was created during the Second World War.

In a memo issued Nov. 2 , Hegseth moved to rename the assistant secretary of defense for special operations and low-intensity conflict to the assistant secretary of war for the Office of Strategic Services.

Significantly, the memo also outlines a move up for the assistant secretary of defense for special operations and low-intensity conflict position to “Code 2,” which is designated exclusively for top-tier senior civilian and military leadership positions, according to the Defense Department . The directive, should it be approved by Congress, would put civilian oversight of special operations forces on par with the service secretaries.

The directive also seeks to expand personnel and funding for SOF at a time when the Pentagon is increasingly utilizing its special operations forces — the January raid to capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, for example. Lawmakers and those inside the SOF themselves are pressing Congress for a greater slice of the defense budget.

“Although the Pentagon is eyeing a 44% overall budget increase to $1.5 trillion in fiscal year 2027, the top-line budget for U.S. Special Operations Command operations and maintenance would rise much more modestly, from $9.7 billion in discretionary spending this fiscal year to $10.9 billion in 2027,” according to a Washington Times article.

“Special operations forces conduct direct…
items.t: Under Hegseth, the OSS rides again — kind of

items.title: VFW seeks veterans’ input on health care experiences in and out of VA
items.summary:
The Veterans of Foreign Wars is conducting a survey of veterans on their health care experiences, including medical treatment received at the Department of Veterans Affairs or in private care. 

Open to all veterans regardless of where they receive medical care, the VFW 2026 Veterans Healthcare Survey seeks to learn about care access, treatment quality, factors that influence medical decisions and overall perceptions of the VA. 

VFW officials said the results will help “identify opportunities to improve” VA health care. 

“We want to hear from veterans who rely on VA for their care, as well as those who have chosen to seek care elsewhere,” Cindy Noel, director of the VFW’s National Veterans Service, said in a statement. “Understanding their experiences and the reason behind their decisions helps us advocate for a healthcare system that better serves the needs of all veterans.”

The survey is open to all veterans regardless of whether they are VFW members or get health care at the VA. The aim is for a broader understanding of how veterans choose their medical care and their experiences, officials said. 

“This survey is specifically measuring veterans experience in VA community care and VA direct care,” Gregg Orto, deputy director for VFW National Veteran Service, told Military Times. ”We want to find out what the veteran is going through from when they make an appointment to how the navigate through the VA system.” 

The VFW, with a membership of more than 1.3 million veterans and supporters, advocates for veterans within the federal government and Congress. Survey…
items.t: VFW seeks veterans’ input on health care experiences in and out of VA

items.title: Trump orders Army to halt Iowa lead detonation plans until courts approve the plan
items.summary:
President Donald Trump ordered the Army to wait for court approval before detonating nearly five tons of lead azide. The directive comes after the acting Secretary of the Army set the controlled explosions for Wednesday, Nov. 25, in defiance of a court stay.

Writing on his social media app Truth Social , Trump said that he supports a controlled detonation of the 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, rather than the risk of an unplanned explosion due to unstable chemicals. However he ordered the Army to pause its plan “ until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward.” He added that the decision is “fully subject” to Governor-Elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation. 

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials,” Trump wrote , adding that he will hold Sand responsible for any death or destruction caused by the lead azide. 

The Army decision to blow up the lead azide barrels on Wednesday came after a federal appeals court granted requests from environmentalists and issued a stay on the detonation on Thursday, effectively pausing it.

The service announced late Sunday in a post on X that the controlled detonation of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026 “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.” 

Dozens of barrels of lead azide — an explosive material used for weapons making at the plant — have degraded and according to the Army are at risk of spontaneous,…
items.t: Army ‘sidesteps’ federal court order, reschedules Iowa munition detonation for Wednesday

items.title: Marines Want Naval Strike Missiles With Double The Range
items.summary:
The U.S. Marine Corps is looking at ways to at least double the range of its ground-launched Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship cruise missiles. NSMs able to hit targets up to 270 nautical miles away, if not more, would significantly increase the area Marine missile batteries could hold at risk . This could be a particular boon in future island-hopping campaigns that are the centerpiece of the Corps’ still-evolving expeditionary and distributed concepts of operations.

The Marines currently field NSM as part of the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS). At NMESIS’ core is the Remotely Operated Ground Unit Expeditionary-Fires (ROGUE-Fires) platform, an uncrewed launcher vehicle based on the 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV). Each ROGUE-Fires launcher can be loaded with up to two NSMs, which come in ready-to-fire canisters, at a time. 

A US Marine Corps ROGUE-Fires launcher vehicle loaded with two NSM launch canisters. USMC 

The NSM is also in U.S. Navy service, primarily on Independence class Littoral Combat Ships (LCS). The stated plan is to eventually arm Freedom class LCSs with these missiles, as well. One Arleigh Burke class destroyer has been equipped with NSM on an as-yet experimental basis. NSM is also in growing service globally in ship-launched and ground-based configurations . 

“The range of the Naval Strike Missile is 135 nautical miles,” a Marine Corps spokesperson recently confirmed to TWZ . “The Marine Corps is currently exploring opportunities to more than double the range of the NSM.”

The 135 nautical mile figure already…
items.t: Marines Want Naval Strike Missiles With Double The Range

items.title: B-2 bomber wings awarded Presidential Unit Citation for Midnight Hammer
items.summary:
Two bomb wings based in Missouri received a President Unit Citation last week for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer.

The 509th Bomb Wing and 131st Bomb Wing were awarded the highest honor a unit can receive in a ceremony presided over by Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach, according to a recent release .

The wings, both housed at Whiteman Air Force Base , received the citation for their “disciplined execution” of Operation Midnight Hammer for mission activities from June 13 to June 22, 2025.

From Whiteman, the largest B-2 Spirit package in history launched on June 21, 2025, traveling to strike Iranian nuclear facilities. The mission took over 36 hours and marked the first combat employment of the bunker-buster bombs, or GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators, which delivered 14 of the 30,000-pound weapons, per the announcement.

The B-2 stealth pilots delivered a total of 420,000 pounds of explosives on two key underground uranium enrichment plants in Iran, while being assisted by a group of refueling tankers and fighter jets.

The mission included 75 precision-guided weapons, such as the 14 bunker-buster bombs deployed by the seven B-2 bombers and over two dozen Tomahawk cruise missiles launched from a U.S. submarine.

Operation Midnight Hammer consisted of a total of 125 aircraft, including the B-2 bombers, F-22 Raptor fighter aircraft and F-35 Lightning stealth strike fighters, as well as KC-135 Stratotanker and KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling aircraft .

“This mission was made possible by over 4,000 Total Force Airmen from hundreds of specialties working…
items.t: B-2 bomber wings awarded Presidential Unit Citation for Midnight Hammer

items.title: China’s Naval Developments Set For The Spotlight At Zhuhai Airshow
items.summary:
China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) says it’s preparing a major presence at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition in Zhuhai, with warships , carrier-based aircraft , advanced weapons systems, and uncrewed platforms set to feature prominently. The expanded naval component will include a new maritime equipment exhibition area at Gaolan Port, located just on the other side of the bay, marking the first time the PLAN has established such a dedicated display at the event.

Zhuhai has become one of the most important events on the international defence and aerospace calendar, serving as China’s principal public showcase for its rapidly developing aviation and military industries. First held in 1996, the biennial China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, commonly known as Airshow China, provides an unusual opportunity to see some of the country’s most advanced military hardware, including aircraft and systems that are rarely shown in such detail elsewhere. While the event also serves as a major platform for China’s aerospace industry to promote its products to potential international customers , it has increasingly become an important venue for revealing new military capabilities and offering glimpses of programs that are otherwise difficult to assess.

A general view of the 15th China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China 2024, at the China International Aviation & Aerospace Exhibition Center on November 15, 2024, in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province of China. Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images

items.title: USS Doris Miller to keep its name, Navy says
items.summary:
The future Ford-class aircraft carrier CVN-81 will remain the USS Doris Miller , the U.S. Navy confirmed.

“There is no intention to change the name of the USS Doris Miller, ” a spokesperson for the secretary of the Navy told Military Times.

In August, speculation over whether the Navy was pivoting to name CVN-81 after President Donald Trump sparked outrage, particularly among Miller’s descendants. Thomas Bledsoe, Miller’s great-nephew, told CNN at the time that the possibility of such a move “was quite a shock.”

When asked in August about the potential pivot, the sea service told Military Times that the “Navy has no announcement to share at this time.”

The confirmation comes as HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding announced the ceremonial keel laying of the Doris Miller on Dec. 5 in Newport News, Virginia. The Navy’s fourth Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, which was initially slated for 2032, was bumped to February 2034 due to “constraints” at the HII shipyard and is projected to take 15 years to complete.

CVN-81 will be the first U.S. aircraft carrier named for a Black American, and the first named in honor of an enlisted sailor. Miller’s namesake was chosen by then-Acting Navy Secretary Thomas Modly in 2019.

Miller, born in rural Texas to sharecroppers and the grandson of slaves, joined the U.S. Navy in September 1939 after struggling to find work in the Jim Crow South.

During that time, Black sailors were not only barred from promotion, but consigned to the messman branch, where they were tasked with the lowly job of making the beds and shining the shoes of…
items.t: USS Doris Miller to keep its name, Navy says

items.title: Army to detonate lead ammunition day before Thanksgiving
items.summary:
The Army has delayed the detonation of an unstable ammunition reserve at an Iowa plant for the second time , the Army announced this weekend, pushing the polarizing move until Wednesday.

Originally scheduled for last week, the service postponed the blasts on Friday until Monday, then rescheduled the operation again. The Army, citing concerns of an uncontrolled explosion, intends to detonate more than 9,000 pounds of degraded lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

The new date will “allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced,” the service said on Sunday on social media , adding that more information would follow. 

Lead azide is a highly sensitive compound used in military detonators and blasting caps. The facility makes medium- and large-caliber ammunition for the Department of Defense. 

Lead is extremely poisonous and, according to the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, there is no safe level of the substance in a person’s bloodstream. Lead can have especially devastating — and sometimes permanent — impacts on pregnant people and young children’s development. 

The community has protested the decision and a bipartisan group of lawmakers are pushing the Army to delay detonation until it can look into alternative disposal methods. 

The Army’s environmental assessment said that the compound could not be chemically degraded, which is an alternative to the blasts, because the lead azide is so sensitive to movement that it might explode unexpectedly.

“The chemical neutralization process requires…
items.t: Army to detonate lead ammunition day before Thanksgiving

items.title: Trump’s contractor gag order is an affront to Congressional oversight
items.summary:
On Friday night, the White House published a new executive order designed to stymie government contractors’ cooperation with the surge in congressional oversight expected to begin once Democrats assume control of Congress in January. The order comes on the heels of the November midterms, when roughly 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to check the president.

The November 20 executive order, “Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting,” requires contractors and their subcontractors to notify the White House and contracting agencies of “any pending or future congressional request” concerning their communications or work with the executive branch. It also requires them to follow instructions to withhold communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.

To ensure compliance, the EO threatens contractors with contract termination and with suspension or debarment—the latter colloquially known as the “corporate death penalty” because it cuts off a contractor’s future government revenue streams.

items.t: Trump’s contractor gag order is an affront to Congressional oversight

items.title: 42-year-old graduates at top of Navy boot camp class
items.summary:
At 40, Christopher Harper was determined to join the Navy. Harper endured numerous phone calls with recruiters, wrote to his Florida congressman, and even took a trip to Mar-a-Lago in search of influential heavy hitters. Thirteen months and multiple waivers later, he arrived at Recruit Training Command, Great Lakes, Illinois, three months after his 42nd birthday. 

“My wife says ‘I don’t know why, Chris, but you don’t like comfort and you ‘ embrace the suck ’ way too much,” Harper told Task & Purpose. 

He doesn’t just seem to embrace it, he seems to thrive on it, having graduated at the top of his class earlier this month and earning the Military Excellence Award , to boot.

“It’s been a 25-year dream to put this uniform on … but I gave that dream up to get married, to have a family, and to go a corporate route, which was what my dad kind of pushed me towards, and so I never thought I’d wear this uniform,” Harper said. “I have a lot of identities. I’ve done a lot in my life, but putting this uniform on is the greatest thing that I’ve done so far, and I’m only three months in. But I could not be more proud and honored to be a part of this.”

“Their actions during Operation Midnight Hammer reflect the constant readiness, precision and professionalism our nation depends on,” Wilsbach said.

items.title: Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US
items.summary:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia—Hours after news broke that the United States would limit defense cooperation with Canada, the Canadian government announced plans to pour 100 million Canadian dollars into a NATO defense-innovation fund. “As far as we're concerned, it's business as usual,” Defense Minister David McGuinty said when asked about the news.

It was a calm reply about an extraordinary development between formerly close allies, but in one sense, it was quite true. As the Trump administration reduces its contributions to the alliance—and in some cases threatens military action against its members—they are increasing their efforts to build their own militaries and industry.

The Canadian decision pushes total commitments to the NATO Innovation Fund past 1.1 billion euros. Joining the fund also makes Canadian defense startups eligible to draw upon it, giving them another source of capital and access to the fund’s network of venture capitalists. 

The NIF is a way to connect startups with investors and military users across the alliance to “help successful solutions reach scale,” Tarja Jaakkola, NATO’s assistant secretary general for defense industry, innovation, and…
items.t: Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US

items.title: USS Theodore Roosevelt Arrives In The Middle East, Relieving USS George Washington
items.summary:
Reinforcements and relief have arrived in the Middle East. USS Theodore Roosevelt chopped into the 5th Fleet-U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility (AOR) and was pictured sailing alongside USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea this week. With USS George H.W. Bush also on station, Roosevelt’s arrival placed three American aircraft carriers in the Middle East, but the overlap was short-lived, as TWZ anticipated . The George Washington Carrier Strike Group (CSG) has left the region, most recently operating at an undisclosed location off India , and has likely begun the journey back to Yokosuka, Japan. With two carriers remaining in the AOR, U.S. carrier force posture remains unchanged.

Meanwhile, the final elements of the Abraham Lincoln CSG that deployed almost a year ago are finally home after completing historic deployments , amphibious assault ship USS Boxer has moved out of the Middle East while her expected replacement, USS Makin Island , is in Singapore, and the acting secretary of the Navy told senators the service will face five years with nine carriers instead of the legally mandated 11.

items.title: The military lacks an ‘overarching plan’ to improve munition stockpiles—partly because it’s no one’s job
items.summary:
The Defense Department has no “overarching plan” to identify, achieve, or measure its progress toward long-term munition production goals, according to a Government Accountability Office study released on Thursday, which said the military was too reactive to global events and unprepared to forecast its own needs.

The GAO cited—among other issues—a lack of centralized authority over weapons inventories, which have been depleted by the Iran war and are vital to U.S. plans for a potential conflict with China.

At the center of the problem lies a discrepancy between what the military can buy and what it actually needs, which the GAO said could even result in munition investments that exceed the Pentagon’s requirements. 

“While DOD is taking steps to focus on munitions shortages, it is not positioned to address these gaps,” the report’s authors wrote. “DOD does not have an overarching plan or designated and empowered leadership to improve munition inventories and meet its munitions requirements. By not identifying long-term goals, strategies to achieve them, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD cannot be sure that its actions will address its munition shortfalls. ”

items.t: The military lacks an ‘overarching plan’ to improve munition stockpiles—partly because it’s no one’s job

items.title: Europeans, with Ukraine’s help, brace for more Russian attacks
items.summary:
IZMIR, Turkey—Vladimir Putin would “love to end the war,” as Donald Trump asserted on Friday, but European NATO members and Ukrainians are working to make sure Russia’s invasion of Ukraine doesn’t end on Moscow’s terms.

In several meetings this week, officials described plans to support their beleaguered European neighbor—and to draw upon the experience to modernize allied militaries and erect new defenses against Russian aggression.

In Berlin on Thursday, the leaders of Germany, France, and Britain reaffirmed NATO’s pledge to provide 70 billion euros’ worth of military equipment, assistance, and training to Ukraine this year—and at least that much in 2027. The European Union has also promised to lend the war-wracked country 60 billion euros for defense and 30 billion for budget support through the next year.

items.title: Navy cargo ship crew honored for rescuing Philippine fishermen
items.summary:
The crew of a Navy supply ship was recognized for saving three Philippine fishermen whose boat was adrift in the South China Sea last winter.

The Chavez was transiting the South China Sea on Jan. 1, 2026, en route to resupply ships in the U.S. 7th Fleet when Third Officer Nicholas Been, who was on watch at the time, spotted the fishermen waving their arms. As a ship in Military Sealift Command, USNS Cesar Chavez is owned by the Navy but crewed mostly by civilians.

The Chavez launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to recover the fishermen, who were brought aboard the supply ship and found to be in good health, according to a Navy press release at the time.

items.title: Oddball CFL-120 Karpat Medium Tank With A Big Gun Faces A Battlefield Increasingly Hostile To Armor
items.summary:
An intriguing new Slovak-Turkish medium tank, the CFL-120 Karpat is designed to appeal to militaries unable to afford or field heavier main battle tanks (MBTs) or have requirements for something lighter and more nimble. But the Karpat arrives at a moment when the survivability of armored vehicles of all kinds is being increasingly questioned , making the case for something of a new class of tank — which combines a 120mm tank gun with a much lighter tracked chassis — far from straightforward.

The Karpat (meaning Carpathians, after the mountain range) made its first public dynamic appearance yesterday at Slovakia’s Záhorie Military Testing Area, demonstrating its mobility off-road and firing its main gun. The vehicle previously made its public debut at the IDEB 2026 defense exhibition in Bratislava earlier this year.

CFL-120 Karpat during trials. CSG UZZIAH R6 

Developed through a partnership involving Slovakia’s Czechoslovak Group (CSG), Turkey’s FNSS, and Italy’s Leonardo, the Karpat combines FNSS’s tracked Kaplan platform with Leonardo’s HITFACT Mk II turret . The latter is armed with a 120mm cannon, giving the vehicle firepower typically associated with much heavier MBTs. The gun is manually loaded, requiring a fourth crew member, although an autoloader could potentially be introduced in the future.

This video provides a backgrounder on the HITFACT Mk II turret, in this case on a Centauro 2 8×8 Mobile Gun System:

items.title: New guide lays out how Army installations can coordinate with local agencies before disaster strikes
items.summary:
The Army relies on local fuel, water, electricity and more to keep its installations going and deploy troops in the face of enemy attacks and natural disasters alike, so the service is urging its 288 camps, posts, and stations to lay that coordination groundwork now, before the balloon goes up.

The service released its Defense Critical Infrastructure community coordination guide Thursday, after its second DCI summit.

“It's a good reminder that readiness is not confined to a motor pool, a runway, or a headquarters building, and it really depends on the civilian and military systems that connect our forces to the nation: power, communication, transportation networks, fuel, water, and ports, just to name a few,” Brandon Pugh, chief of staff to the acting Army secretary, told reporters.

The guide suggests ways that Army installation officials can coordinate with local governments, utilities, and other services to keep communication open in case of disaster.

To that end, the Army has held two DCI summits this year, the first in May at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and the second at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, on Thursday.

items.title: Marine who survived Fallujah’s ‘Hell House’ under NCIS investigation

Retired Marine Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, a Navy Cross recipient who is perhaps best known for an iconic photo taken of him emerging from the “Hell House” during the Second Battle of Fallujah in the Iraq War, is under federal investigation, Task & Purpose has confirmed.

Kasal served in the Marine Corps from 1984 until his retirement in 2018. 

On Nov. 13, 2004, in Fallujah, Iraq, Marines with 3rd Battalion, 1st Marine Regiment, went street-to-street in deadly and unforgiving house-to-house combat. As Kasal and his fellow Marines cleared the house in order to reach those pinned inside, he was repeatedly wounded — and in one case, he used his body to shield another Marine from a grenade blast. Kasal emerged from the building, bloody, gripping his sidearm and held…

items.title: As the Air Force tries to protect its F-35s from drones, former airmen say it highlights the risks for maintenance crews

The Air Force is turning to nets to prevent drones from destroying its most sensitive fighter jets. Former aircraft maintainers told Task & Purpose that it highlights the risks that drones also pose to the personnel who fix and sustain them.

In recent months, two Air Force bases with units that fly highly sensitive fighter jets have sought input from private contractors on using nets to protect aircraft and personnel from small drones. The solicitations come as the U.S. figures out how to address a flurry of drone incursions on its bases at home and at installations abroad .

In March, officials at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, where the 20th Fighter Wing flies F-16s, sought to add nets to their aircraft sunshades to “prevent intrusions” from small drones.

Earlier this month, Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida posted a market research solicitation asking private companies to pitch nets for the sunshades shielding their F-35s along the flight line. The objective, according to the Tyndall notice, is to prevent small drones from “penetrating the interior of the sunshade structures to protect aircraft and personnel.” 

Chris McGhee, a former F-16 aircraft maintainer, said that although the solicitation highlights force protection, in reality, maintainers are still at risk. 

“The aircraft is certainly going to be much safer than if there was no netting and the drone came in direct contact with the hull of the aircraft, the skin of the aircraft. But when I think about the aircraft maintainers working around the aircraft, they are going to be traveling in and out of…
items.t: As the Air Force tries to protect its F-35s from drones, former airmen say it highlights the risks for maintenance crews

items.title: The Jet That Always Shadows Air Force One When The President Travels Abroad
items.summary:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent visit to China has drawn particular attention from online flight trackers. This is in no small part due to the fact that all three of the U.S. Air Force’s current Boeing 747-based Air Force One aircraft – the two older VC-25As and the new ex-Qatari VC-25B “Bridge” jet – have supported the trip. Another militarized 747, an E-4B Nightwatch , commonly referred to as a ‘doomsday plane,’ was also spotted shadowing the group to and from Asia. 

While this drew a lot of attention online, including blog posts from defense-focused sites, the reality is this is absolutely standard practice. The E-4B is just another part, albeit a very unique and shy one, of the massive aerial logistics ballet that occurs whenever the President leaves the country.

The Air Force currently has four E-4Bs, also known as National Airborne Operations Centers (NAOC), all based at Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. Based on the 747-200 model, three of these planes first entered service in the 1970s as E-4A Advanced Airborne Command Posts (AACP). Those aircraft were subsequently brought up to the E-4B NAOC standard in the 1980s, and were eventually joined by a fourth example converted straight to that configuration. The jets have been continuously upgraded over the years. In addition to supporting presidential travel, the Nightwatch aircraft also regularly transport the Secretary of Defense (now also referred to as the Secretary of War) and their staff during overseas trips, among other roles.

A stock picture of an E-4B Nightwatch jet. US Military

items.title: Regent Squire Wing-In-Ground Effect Drone To Patrol Middle East Waters
items.summary:
Regent has reached a deal to sell an unspecified number of its autonomous Squire Seagliders to a U.S. government customer, Regent CEO Billy Thalheimer announced on X . The electric-powered drones will make up “a small fleet that will be deployed in the Middle East next year, doing multi-domain perception” for that customer, Thalheimer stated in his post. He declined to name the customer, the number of drones involved or the value of the contract, and so did the communications arm of his Rhode Island-based company when we asked.

The Regent Squire Seaglider in flight. (Regent) 

What makes the Squire unique is that it is what is known as a hydrofoiling wing-in-ground (WIG) effect craft.

The WIG drone uses a hydrofoil to get airborne and then cruise in the air at an altitude of about one wingspan above the water. These ground-effect flights are designed to take advantage of the cusion of air compressed between the wings and the surface, providing a sweet spot of increased lift and reduced drag. In theory, this should provide the Squire with high efficiency and relevant speed, all without needing to operate from a traditional runway .

Regent describes the Squire as a “drone that flies in ground effect below radar line of sight at up to 70 knots, with a planned range of more than 100 nautical miles and a 50-pound configurable payload for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), logistics, search and rescue, and anti-submarine warfare.”

In his post, Thalheimer notes that “combined with various sensors, Squire can do multiple on-water perception and…
items.t: Regent Squire Wing-In-Ground Effect Drone To Patrol Middle East Waters

A major takeaway from Project Flytrap, a Poland-based exercise, is that the way combat units, communications units, and headquarters share information and make decisions can’t keep up, according to a junior signal officer who helped manage data for the exercise earlier this year.

It’s a gap artificial intelligence could potentially fill, Glazer said,…

items.title: ‘I was seriously wrong’: Experts say superintelligent AI may arrive as soon as next year
items.summary:
Some forecasters who closely track AI developments have drastically revised predictions this month, saying that “artificial superintelligence” may arrive years earlier than they thought. 

Sentinel, a forecasting group, now expects superhuman AI to arrive around 2028, not 2031. The AI Futures Project, which last year laid out a scenario in which superintelligent AI might arrive in 2027, says development is proceeding faster than the scenario assumed. 

Both groups changed their predictions in response to a Nov. 5 report by METR, a nonprofit that evaluates AI risks. METR found that the speed at which AI models were improving within AI developer Anthropic had roughly doubled since late last year, which it attributed mostly to the extensive use of AI agents to help with research. 

Some experts think AI-driven research could start a runaway loop of AI improving itself, known as recursive self-improvement, a threat they say demands quick action.

items.title: Why the Army is detonating explosives at an Iowa munitions plant
items.summary:
The Army plans to detonate 68 drums of explosive materials near a small Iowa town on Friday, and is advising nearby residents to prepare for loud noises, potential window damage and a dust plume that may contain some lead. However, the plan and the potential for an airborne dust cloud have some residents concerned and prompted several schools to announce closures.

The Army will detonate approximately 5 tons of lead azide on Friday, which is stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Several barrels containing lead azide — an explosive material — have been stored at the facility for decades and now show signs of deterioration. The chemicals have started to crystallize, making them more unstable and capable of potentially detonating on their own.

The two detonations are set for noon Central Time on Friday. The barrels will be detonated in a controlled space, surrounded by sand and concrete barriers. The Army is warning residents of loud noises and ground vibrations.

According to the latest public advisory , released Wednesday, some residents in Middletown have been asked to evacuate from 8 a.m. to2 p.m. on Friday, due to the possibility of shockwaves that could damage windows. The Army said that the Armed Forces Reserve Center in town is available for Middletown residents if they need a place to stay.

The plant, part of the Army Joint Munitions Command, is near Middletown, a town of roughly 400 people. In March, a safety review found that the lead azide was unstable. The Army began working with state and federal partners to devise a plan to dispose of the…
items.t: Why the Army is detonating explosives at an Iowa munitions plant

But the countries still operating the Mirage 2000 — the Rafale’s predecessor — have their own reasons to hold on to them.

Ukraine’s latest appeal came during the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in Brussels on November 17. President Volodymyr Zelensky asked for 40 more F-16s , citing the time existing aircraft spend undergoing maintenance and repairs, an issue you can read about here . But Zelensky also called on European partners to provide additional Mirage fighters, arguing that they could be put to work more quickly than Rafales, which require more training and preparation. He did not specify how many Mirages Ukraine wants. At this point, however, any single airframe would likely be accepted, whether it can be used in a frontline capacity or only as a source of spare parts.

items.title: Impacts Of Latest Neptune Missile Strike On Kerch Bridge Seen In Satellite Imagery
items.summary:
TWZ has obtained satellite imagery taken today of the Kerch Bridge. It shows damage from recent strikes to the rail span, as well as the section of the road span that was knocked out earlier in the week . The rail line was hit again just overnight , bringing train traffic across this vital Russian logistics conduit to a halt for a time. Readers can get caught up first on what was already known about the third Ukrainian strike on the bridge in now four days in our initial reporting .

Vantor’s WorldView-1 satellite captured the image, seen in part at the top of this story and below, at 1:51 PM local time. At least two, and possibly three, impact points are visible on the rail span. From what we can see, the damage looks to be limited to only one of the two sets of tracks on the bridge. 

The WorldView-1 satellite image of Kerch Bridge, taken on November 19, 2026, showing impact points on the rail span to the left of the arch. The section of the road span that was destroyed on the night of November 16-17 is also visible here. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor 

A large scorch mark is also seen on one corner of an arch that goes across part of the rail span. However, this damage does not appear to be new based on previous satellite imagery, as well as pictures and video taken at surface level. 

A side-by-side comparison of the scorch mark on the arch as seen in the image from Vantor, at left, and in a picture that emerged online following the strikes on Kerch Bridge on November 16-17, at right. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor /via X

items.title: New Army contract for bunkers in Middle East cites ‘extreme operational urgency’
items.summary:
The Army urgently needs to build concrete bunkers to replace shipping containers and T-walls that troops are using to shelter from drones across the Middle East, contract documents show.

The service needs contractors to build “fully operational indirect fire” bunkers in 45 days “due to extreme operational urgency,” according to a solicitation posted Nov. 13 to the federal government’s contracting database. 

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters,” Army officials wrote in contracting documents. “The objective is to safeguard U.S. and Coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in the [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility.” 

The Army also asked contractors to demolish and dispose of “non-standard bunkers” (identified as “converted” shipping containers), T-walls, and “scrap obstacles” in order to make room for the new concrete structures. The concrete buildings will also have sandbag reinforcements — a modification that troops have made to shelters in recent years to mitigate blast overpressure waves . 

In all, contract documents indicate that the service needs five bunkers at two bases in Saudi Arabia, 47 at two sites in Lebanon and 10 at a site in Israel. Army Times’ Michael Peck was first to report on the contract posting.

The bunker solicitation comes as questions have been raised about whether U.S. bases had adequate shelters and overall force protection measures in the region when the war…
items.t: New Army contract for bunkers in Middle East cites ‘extreme operational urgency’

items.title: Defense Business Brief: Vantor’s Raptor; Hadrian’s foundry, and more
items.summary:
Flying drones at lower altitudes can help them evade radar detection, but what happens if the GPS is jammed? How will the drone know where it is?

“The lower you go, the more important it is that you're looking out obliquely…you need to have a 3D reference in order to be able to compare to, to determine your position,” Paul Millhouse, Vantor’s senior director who leads the Raptor program, told Defense One. 

Drones typically use vision-based positioning informed by two-dimensional maps that display an area from an overhead perspective, Millhouse explained. But buildings can become more than just rooftops in a drone’s line of sight when flying low through a cityscape at lower altitudes. 

Using its three-dimensional satellite imagery, Vantor built its Raptor technology to be a GPS alternative so drones can navigate even if signals are jammed. The technology uses a video feed from the drone’s on-board camera and an initial estimate of that camera’s position and altitude, which is maintained by the drone’s navigation system.

The company first debuted the product last year and has been busy flight testing and integrating it in “live, real GPS-jammed environments,” including long-range operations…
items.t: Defense Business Brief: Vantor’s Raptor; Hadrian’s foundry, and more

items.title: USS George Washington leaves the Middle East as replacement carrier arrives
items.summary:
The USS George Washington left the Middle East after three months in the region, the Navy confirmed on Wednesday.

The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier departed the 5th Fleet area of operations and entered the 7th Fleet’s region, the Navy said, where it is set to conduct “routine operations,” a Pacific Fleet spokesperson said in a statement to Task & Purpose.

The carrier’s exit from the Middle East comes after the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the region only days prior. The ship entered the area amid renewed, if low-scale, fighting between the United States and Iran.

The USS George Washington arrived in the 5th Fleet area of operations in August, after sailing in the South China Sea. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left its homeport in September, sailing in the Pacific before it was confirmed to head to the Middle East. The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in the spring, has been active in the area since then, barring a brief port stop in Thailand in early October.

USNI News first reported on the USS George Washington leaving the Middle East.

The USS George Washington sails alongside the USS Theodore Roosevelt on Nov. 16, 2026. Navy photo. 

Photos posted by the Navy showed the USS George Washington sailing alongside the USS Theodore Roosevelt on Nov. 15. It had been expected that the George Washington would be leaving the area once a new carrier arrived.

items.t: USS George Washington leaves the Middle East as replacement carrier arrives

items.summary:
Cuts – which exclude shop floor and aircraft maintenance – prompt calls for more orders to support British defence contractor

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, prompting calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

items.title: Appropriators slash Trump’s $17B Golden Dome request in draft bill
items.summary:
Senate appropriators reined in President Donald Trump's $17 billion-plus Golden Dome ask this week, pushing roughly half the administration’s request into a draft defense bill that budget experts said is unlikely to pass, signaling that long-term funding for the missile-defense system can’t rely on a one-time measure facing uncertainty in the lame-duck Congress.

The nearly $1.1 trillion proposal released by the GOP-led Senate Appropriations Committee on Monday contains tens of billions in funding for priority defense programs—including Golden Dome—that the administration has been zealously campaigning for via a $350 billion reconciliation measure, one dogged by backlash over Iran war spending.

Nearly all of the $17.5 billion Golden Dome request is tied up in reconciliation, making it particularly vulnerable to funding uncertainty, as the program’s Space Force lead acknowledged as far back as August. Only about $398 million of the administration’s base budget request was allocated for the program.

As GOP lawmakers scramble to push the administration’s defense priorities through before a Democratic majority takes Congress in January, appropriators tagged nearly $9.4 billion for Golden Dome in their fiscal 2027 defense draft—a steadier funding vehicle—saying the administration’s reliance on reconciliation measures “threatens the success” of the program

items.t: Appropriators slash Trump’s $17B Golden Dome request in draft bill

items.title: Ukraine Strikes Kerch Bridge Once Again: Crimea Governor (Updated)
items.summary:
Ukraine has carried out another attack on the already badly damaged Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov. The latest strike took place two days after a large section of the span was destroyed in a complex missile and drone attack.

Tuesday’s operation took out the road bridge span but left the rail span still standing. Amazingly trains were still running despite the remaining side being pummeled by weapons over two nights and clearly damaged. Dropping the rail portion would sever the vital conduit between Crimea and Russia entirely.

Video from a Russian passenger train passing the section of the Kerch Bridge road span that was destroyed by Ukrainian drones/missiles. pic.twitter.com/NypzkoD0Of 

— Mike Eckel (@Mike_Eckel) November 18, 2026 

“As a result of another attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily suspended,” Aksyonov stated on Telegram , using the Russian term for the bridge. “All relevant services are on duty. An assessment of the damage is underway. Further information will be provided as it becomes available.”

So far, Ukrainian authorities haven’t commented on the attack. We have reached out to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s office, the Security Service of Ukraine and the Unmanned Systems Command for more details.

This latest strike follows what Zelensky described as a weeks-long phased operation that took out a huge chunk of the bridge and one of its supporting arches in the early morning hours Tuesday local time. He also said this was in retaliation for Russia’s continued strikes on…
items.t: Ukraine Strikes Kerch Bridge Once Again: Crimea Governor

items.title: The Coast Guard icebreaker nobody wanted just came back from a 133-day Arctic patrol
items.summary:
Second chances don’t come around too often, but they did for the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Storis, an icebreaker that started life as a failed towboat for offshore oil rigs but joined America’s maritime security service in 2024–despite one Coast Guard admiral saying at one point that the ship “may, at best, marginally meet our requirements.”

On Saturday, the ship returned to its temporary home port of Seattle after a 133-day, 17,000-nautical-mile deployment where Storis was the only U.S. surface ship in the High Arctic , the region’s northernmost section, according to a Coast Guard press release .

Along the way, the crew carried out the first law enforcement mission by an icebreaker in more than 20 years when they inspected fishing boats in the Bering Sea. They also practiced firing machine guns in extreme cold conditions; escorted a grounded fishing vessel to safety; tested out small drones in extreme cold and at high latitudes; and monitored Chinese-flagged research vessels, which experts say gather oceanographic information for China’s scientific, commercial and military fleets.
